justice: The street allocates substantial space to motor traffic, with multiple wide vehicle lanes visible in the foreground and mid-distance, indicating stronger provision for drivers than for slower users.

Tree-lined side verges on both sides provide some environmental benefit to all users, but the pedestrian realm itself is visually recessed behind planting strips and not strongly prioritized in the street composition.
A central metal fence divides directions of travel and organizes vehicle movement fairly, yet no visible dedicated cycle lane or clearly marked pedestrian crossing appears in the image.

The roadway surface is smooth and lane markings are clear for drivers, but accessibility for non-motorized users cannot be fully confirmed because curb ramps, tactile paving, and sidewalk access points are not visible.
safety: The broad carriageway has clear lane markings, good sightlines, and limited visible congestion, which supports predictable vehicle movement and reduces immediate crash risk for drivers.
A continuous central guard fence helps prevent unsafe mid-block crossing and separates opposing traffic streams, improving overall traffic order.
Streetlights are present along the corridor, which suggests some nighttime safety infrastructure, though their performance cannot be verified from this daytime image.

The high design speed implied by the wide straight road may create risk for pedestrians and cyclists if crossing points are infrequent, especially since no zebra crossing or traffic-calming feature is visible here.
livability: Mature trees along both sides and landscaped medians create a greener residential boulevard condition, which improves everyday environmental quality.
Tall residential towers directly front the corridor, suggesting substantial housing supply and a neighborhood with regular daily use rather than an isolated arterial.
The street feels orderly and clean, with maintained pavement, trimmed planting, and little visible clutter, which supports a stable living environment.
However, the image shows limited active ground-floor frontage, seating, or visible public gathering spaces, so social vibrancy at street level appears modest.
sustainability: The extensive rows of trees on both sides contribute shade, carbon uptake, and air-quality improvement, indicating meaningful green infrastructure.
Dense high-rise housing along the corridor suggests compact urban form, which can support shorter trips and more efficient land use.
The landscaped strips and planted edges reduce the visual dominance of asphalt somewhat and may help with stormwater absorption compared with a fully hardscaped edge.
Even so, the corridor remains heavily road-oriented, with large paved vehicle surfaces and no visible dedicated bus lane or bicycle facility to strongly support low-carbon mode shift.
aesthetics: The boulevard has strong visual order, with evenly spaced streetlights, aligned tower blocks, and a long central perspective that gives the street a coherent appearance.
Lush green tree canopies on the right side and consistent planting along both edges soften the large scale of the buildings and roadway.
The buildings appear well maintained, with relatively uniform color tones and façade rhythm, contributing to a neat and upscale residential image.
The road surface and barriers are also clean and orderly, although the very wide asphalt corridor slightly reduces human-scale visual warmth.
comfort: Tree cover along both sides offers some thermal relief for people on side paths and sidewalks, especially compared with a fully exposed boulevard.
The asphalt carriageway itself is broad and sun-exposed, so users outside the shaded edges may still experience heat buildup in warm weather.
The pavement visible for vehicles appears smooth and well maintained, which improves physical comfort for drivers and likely reduces vibration and noise.
Psychological comfort benefits from the open sightlines, low visible crowding, and tidy streetscape, but the oversized road width may feel less comfortable for pedestrians due to traffic scale.
walkability: Sidewalks are not prominently visible from this camera position, and the street cross-section is dominated by several traffic lanes, which weakens the pedestrian priority of the corridor.
The central guard fence prevents informal crossing and can improve safety, but it also reduces direct pedestrian permeability if formal crossings are spaced far apart.
Street trees along both sides likely improve walking conditions on the margins by adding shade and greenery.
No visible zebra crossing, curb extension, median refuge opening, or pedestrian-focused signage is present in the image, so crossing convenience appears limited.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, painted cycle marking, or physically protected cycling facility is visible on either side of the roadway.
The wide, fast-looking multi-lane carriageway likely creates stress for on-road cycling, especially for less confident riders.
The central fence improves traffic order for motor vehicles but does not provide any evident support for bicycle crossing or protected cycle movement.
There is also no visible bicycle parking, bike signal, or curbside micro-mobility space, indicating weak cycling accommodation.
